chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 271 to 280, Kapilar's kurinji decade of the monkey (குரக்குப் பத்து): each poem opens on a monkey of the hill lord's slope (the stuffed-cheeked female, the reckless young at the honey or the bamboo top, the male who carries his mate from the tiger or beats the rain bubbles) and turns it on the lord: his constancy, his night visits, his leaving, the beauty he took, the gossip he will raise, and the marriage the friend demands.

271.reading: The friend says that the lord of the land where a female monkey that has eaten avarai beans looks like a trader's stuffed bag could have many fresh young women if he wanted them, but because he is her old kinsman he stays kind to this girl.
271.nuance: The comic image of the greedy monkey with bulging cheeks stands beside the claim that the lord does not grab every woman he could have: what holds him is the old tie (தொல்கேள்), so the friend grounds his constancy in kinship rather than in passion.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey and the hill lord fix the kurinji slope

comparisons.tenor: the female monkey with cheeks full of beans

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the girl is spoken of as இவள் and the lord in the third person, so the friend is taken to be vouching for him to the foster mother; she may as well be reassuring the girl herself

272.reading: The girl tells her friend that the lord of the land where the untaught young of the black-fingered female monkey leaps onto the fearsome tall branch beside the sweet honey of the steep cliff does not know what coming by night means, and that her mother keeps saying 'he will come, he will come'.
272.nuance: The untaught young monkey (கல்லா) that leaps at the dangerous branch beside the honey answers the lord who 'does not know' (அறியான்) the danger of the night path; that is a near-miss ullurai, left as scene because the closing lines cannot be fixed: whether the mother's 'he will come' means she has guessed the night visits or expects a suitor changes the situation the image would point to.

thinai_evidence.note: monkey, cliff and wild honey are the hill's things

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the vocative தோழி and யாய் (my mother) make the girl the speaker

273.reading: The friend tells the lord of the good hill, where the strong young of the dull-headed female monkey feed on the coral-bright shoots of the asoka by the path, that if he goes away, she who lives on her love for him will weep even more than the friend herself.
273.nuance: The friend measures the girl's grief against her own (என்னினும்): she admits she too will weep, so the plea is made from inside the shared household of the two girls, not as a go-between's tactic.

thinai_evidence.note: the asoka, the monkey and the good hill place it on the kurinji slope; the parting is the brief absence of kalavu

comparisons.tenor: the bright young shoots of the asoka

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and hearer are inferred from the poem's address

274.reading: The girl tells her friend that the lord of the land where the untaught male, husband of the female monkey, hurries up the high slope together with her when the bright-striped tiger roars has gone away, taking with him the beauty of her soft shoulders and her sleep.
274.nuance: கல்லா (untaught) is pointed: the creature that has learnt nothing still keeps his mate beside him, so the lord's leaving reads as a failure of what even a beast knows.

thinai_evidence.note: monkey, tiger and the high slope are the hill's things; the parting is within kalavu

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the vocative தோழி and என் மெல்தோள் make the girl the speaker

iraicchi.act: at the tiger's roar the male monkey, called the female's husband, hurries up the slope together with her (உடன்)
iraicchi.sense: even the untaught monkey takes his mate with him out of danger, while the lord went off alone and took only her beauty and her sleep

275.reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the red-furred male monkey, leader of the troop, beats the rain bubbles on the wide rock with a little cane stick that, though the girls desire him, their fine beauty would not fade if he would only be gracious.
275.nuance: The monkey smashing the fragile rain bubbles for play sits close to the girl's beauty that fades while the lord delays, a near-miss ullurai: only one correspondence (careless play breaking something fragile) can be named, so it fails condition 3. The friend's question turns his grace (அருள்) into the cure: marriage, not desire, keeps beauty.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey, the cane and the broad rock of the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and hearer are inferred from the poem's address

276.reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the leaf-eating male monkey, the female's lover, beats the swelling young clouds on the wide rock with a cool fragrant narai creeper: even if he does not love her, let him marry her before he goes, so that she is called the wife of the lord of the good hill where vengai blooms in the rock clefts.
276.nuance: நயவாய் ஆயினும் is startling: the friend concedes he may not love her and still asks for marriage, so what she wants for the girl is the name (பெண்டு எனப் படுத்து), the public standing that protects her, more than his feeling. The vengai in bloom is the hill's marriage season.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey, the vengai and the good hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and hearer are inferred from the poem's address

277.reading: The friend tells the lord of the hill, where the untaught female monkey frolics with her male on the boulder in the hunters' yard that the beasts rub against: let him never leave the girl so that pallor spreads over her eyes, which rival the blue lily growing in the pond.
277.nuance: The monkeys play right beside human dwellings (குறவர் முன்றில்), so the pair is a sight the lord passes every time he comes: the friend's warning is set on his own doorstep.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunters' yard, the monkey and the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and hearer are inferred from the poem's address

iraicchi.act: the female monkey stays and plays with her male on the boulder of the hunters' yard
iraicchi.sense: the beasts of his own hill keep to their mates, so the lord should never leave the girl and let her eyes grow pale

278.reading: The friend says that the lord of the land, where the jointed bamboo of the slope, once the strong young monkey has leapt off it, springs up like a fishing rod that jerks a fish out of the pool, has given the girl a sickness those who suffer it never forget and has taken the beauty onlookers never tire of.
278.nuance: The fishing-rod simile is the key: the bamboo does not merely spring back, it springs back like a rod that has just landed a fish, so the image already contains the taking (கொண்டனன்) the closing line names.

thinai_evidence.note: the slope, the bamboo and the monkey

comparisons.tenor: the bamboo stem springing up when the young monkey leaps off

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the lord and the girl are both in the third person and the girl's beauty is praised as one onlookers never tire of, so the friend is taken to be explaining the girl's sickness to the mother; the girl speaking to her friend is the other reading

ullurai.tenor: the lord who has had his joy of the girl and gone off unchanged

pairs.situation: he has leapt away from her once his pleasure was taken
he springs back upright and untouched while she is left with the sickness
he has hooked her beauty and carried it off

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the bamboo and the young monkey of the kurinji slope in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

279.reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the female monkey, having climbed the clinging itti tree that spreads over the rock and grazed on wild jasmine, frolics with her mate on the hillside, that if he comes, their village lies within the rocks and its whispering street will turn to open gossip.
279.nuance: அம்பல் (the murmur) and அலர் (the spoken gossip) are two stages of the same talk: the friend warns that his next visit will turn the first into the second.

thinai_evidence.note: the rock fig, the wild jasmine and the hillside

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and hearer are inferred from the poem's address

iraicchi.act: the female monkey plays openly with her mate (துணையோடு) on the hillside
iraicchi.sense: the beasts may be together in plain sight, while the lovers' meetings set the village whispering, so only marriage will let them be together openly

280.reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the untaught strong young of the black-fingered female monkey, climbing the tall green bamboo, seems to beat the moon with a little stick: hearing that he would marry, did she not tell it to her mother?
280.nuance: The monkey reaching for the moon is a joke about overreach, and the friend's question turns it on herself: she spoke to her mother on the strength of his word, so if he now delays she is the one left beating at the moon.

thinai_evidence.note: monkey and bamboo of the hill

comparisons.tenor: the young monkey with a stick on the bamboo top

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the address நாட and என் யாய் (my mother, the girl's foster mother) make the friend the speaker

links.note: Natrinai 168 and Ainkurunuru 273 share a formula: the young of the dull-headed female monkey feeding on the good hill and the girl called நின் நயந்து உறைவி; in Natrinai 168 the friend uses it to forbid his coming at midnight, in Ainkurunuru 273 to forbid his going away.
links.teaches: The same formula serves to stop the lover coming and to stop him leaving, which shows the double bind of secret love: the girl's life is staked both on the danger of his night visits and on his absence, and only marriage ends both.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 69 a widowed female monkey leaps from the ridge to her death and the friend begs the lover not to come at midnight; in Ainkurunuru 274 the male monkey carries his mate up the slope from the roaring tiger while the girl's lover has gone away.
links.teaches: Read together, the monkey couple names both fears of secret love: in Kuruntokai the girl would not survive losing him to the night path, in Ainkurunuru she is left by a man less faithful than the beast that shields its mate, so the danger lies as much in his leaving as in his coming.

links.note: Kural 1183 has the woman say he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; Ainkurunuru 278 says the lord gave a sickness never forgotten and took the beauty onlookers never tired of.
links.teaches: Valluvar keeps only the exchange as the woman's own complaint, while the Sangam poem sets it in an image of a bamboo springing back like a rod that has landed a fish, which shows the taking and the man's unharmed recoil that the couplet's bare bargain leaves out.

links.note: In Natrinai 334 the monkeys frolic with their male in the falls and the friend fears for the girl's life if the lover comes through the stormy night; in Ainkurunuru 279 the female monkey frolics with her mate and the friend warns that his coming will set the village gossiping.
links.teaches: Under the same image of monkeys at play with their mates, the friend has two separate reasons to keep the lover away, the night path's danger in Natrinai and the village tongue in Ainkurunuru, so the pair shows that the creatures' open play stands for exactly the freedom secret love lacks on both counts.

links.note: In Ainkurunuru 103 the friend tells the mother that the shore lord has become fit for the girl and she for him; in Ainkurunuru 280 the friend reminds the hill lord that on hearing he would marry she told her mother.
links.teaches: The neythal decade stages the friend's disclosure to the mother, and Kapilar's poem shows its price: she spoke only on the strength of the man's word, so her standing at home now hangs on his keeping it.

source_issues: 271-280: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade, so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem's address.
271: the word division பகர்வர் / பக்கின் across lines 1 and 2 and the sense of பல்பசுப் பெண்டிர் are hard; the reading takes பக்கு as the traders' bag and பசு as 'fresh'.
272: line 4 அறியான் is masculine and leaves open who does not know and whether the mother's 'he will come' (line 5) means she has guessed the night visits; the reading cannot be fixed.
275: line 1 குரங்கின் தலிஅவன் looks corrupt (likely தலைவன், the troop's leader); the reading follows that sense.
279: line 4 கல்லகத் ததுஎம் and 280: line 3 மதிபுடைப் பதுபோல carry word breaks in the middle of words (கல்லகத்தது, மதிபுடைப்பது); the readings join them.
273, 274, 275, 278, 279: the shown text carries repaired lines (flags in show); the readings follow the repaired text.
